prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit.

We represent: defendant officer.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that an officer's use of a taser on an actively resisting suspect does not violate clearly established Fourth Amendment law.

Cite at least six decisions of the Sixth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.
answer:
## ARGUMENT

### THE OFFICER IS ENTITLED TO QUALIFIED IMMUNITY BECAUSE USING A TASER ON AN ACTIVELY RESISTING SUSPECT DOES NOT VIOLATE CLEARLY ESTABLISHED FOURTH AMENDMENT LAW.

Qualified immunity shields officers from civil liability unless the plaintiff shows that (1) the officer violated a constitutional right that (2) was "clearly established" at the time. *Ashcroft v. al-Kidd*, 563 U.S. 731, 735 (2011). A right is clearly established only if its contours are "sufficiently clear that every reasonable official would have understood that what he is doing violates that right." *Id.* at 741 (cleaned up). Courts must not define clearly established law "at a high level of generality." *Id.* at 742. The inquiry requires "a high degree of specificity," particularly in excessive-force cases, where the result "depends very much on the facts of each case." *District of Columbia v. Wesby*, 583 U.S. 48, 63–64 (2018) (cleaned up). The plaintiff bears the burden of showing that the right was clearly established. *Baynes v. Cleland*, 799 F.3d 600, 610 (6th Cir. 2015).

**A. The use of force was objectively reasonable under *Graham*.**

Excessive-force claims are judged by objective reasonableness, considering "the severity of the crime at issue, whether the suspect poses an immediate threat to the safety of the officers or others, and whether he is actively resisting arrest or attempting to evade arrest by flight." *Graham v. Connor*, 490 U.S. 386, 396 (1989). This Court has repeatedly held that an officer may use a taser against a suspect who actively resists. *See Hagans v. Franklin Cnty. Sheriff's Off.*, 695 F.3d 505, 509–10 (6th Cir. 2012); *Rudlaff v. Gillispie*, 791 F.3d 638, 641–43 (6th Cir. 2015). The cases denying immunity involve suspects who were not resisting at all, or who had already been subdued. *See Goodwin v. City of Painesville*, 781 F.3d 314, 326–28 (6th Cir. 2015); *Roell v. Hamilton Cnty.*, 870 F.3d 471, 482–84 (6th Cir. 2017); *Austin v. Redford Twp. Police Dep't*, 690 F.3d 490, 498–99 (6th Cir. 2012).

This Court draws that line using the concept of "active resistance," which includes "physically struggling with, threatening, or disobeying officers." *Goodwin*, 781 F.3d at 327 (cleaned up). Here, [Plaintiff] [describe conduct: pulled away, refused to place hands behind back, tensed, struck at officers, etc.] after receiving repeated commands. [JA __.] That conduct is active resistance. The Officer used the taser only after lesser efforts to gain compliance failed, and ceased once [Plaintiff] was under control. [JA __.] Force that is proportionate to continued physical resistance is reasonable. *See Hagans*, 695 F.3d at 509–10; *Rudlaff*, 791 F.3d at 641–43.

**B. No clearly established law placed the unlawfulness of the Officer's conduct beyond debate.**

Even if a jury might view the force as excessive, the Officer is still immune. In *Hagans*, this Court granted immunity to an officer who used a taser on a suspect who refused to comply with commands, because no clearly established law prohibited that use of force. 695 F.3d at 509–11. In *Rudlaff*, the Court again granted immunity where officers tased a resisting suspect, explaining that the plaintiff identified no controlling authority forbidding the tasing of a suspect who had not submitted to officers' control. 791 F.3d at 641–43.

The decisions on which Plaintiff will rely are distinguishable on the facts. In *Goodwin*, the suspect was not resisting and was tased repeatedly, and this Court noted that mere noncompliance, without more, does not amount to active resistance. 781 F.3d at 326–28. In *Roell*, the suspect was restrained and no longer posed a threat. 870 F.3d at 482–84. In *Austin*, the suspect had stopped resisting before force was applied. 690 F.3d at 498–99. Those decisions establish, at most, that force against a compliant or subdued person is unlawful. They do not "squarely govern" the situation of an officer confronting a suspect who is physically resisting. *Mullenix v. Luna*, 577 U.S. 7, 13 (2015) (per curiam) (cleaned up). Because the Officer's conduct fell on the permissible side of the line this Court has drawn, a reasonable officer would not have known that using a taser here was unlawful. *See Brown v. Chapman*, 814 F.3d 447, 457–60 (6th Cir. 2016).

**C. Conclusion.**

The Officer faced a suspect who was actively resisting, and Plaintiff cannot identify controlling authority that clearly forbade the force used. The judgment denying qualified immunity should be reversed.
